body:
I was reading [Why Rust powers Temporal’s Core SDK](https://temporal.io/blog/why-rust-powers-core-sdk) and learned that the Core SDK serves as the foundation for the TypeScript, Python, .NET, and Ruby SDKs. I’m curious why the Go SDK isn’t built on top of the Rust Core SDK—are there technical limitations or business considerations behind this choice?

We’ve faced similar challenges as mentioned in the article and are interested in trying this approach. Since we also want to support a Go SDK, we’d love to hear any lessons learned or considerations when building a Go SDK on top of the Rust Core SDK.

comments.body:
The Go SDK was built before we built the Rust Core (Java is the oldest, Go is 2nd), so changing it to use Rust core would require maintaining 2 versions (this pure Go and a Rust-core Go SDK), due to backwards compatibility (Metrics in Go and Java don't align 1:1 with Core-based SDK's, as well as certain details with how histories are created).

From a technical side, Go has a very poor native compilation story and poor shared library distribution story.

Not to say there will _never_ be a Go SDK on top of core, but no current plans to build this.
Closing this issue as not really an issue but a discussion topic. Feel free to join us on the `#go-sdk` channel on [Slack](https://t.mp/slack) or [the forum](https://community.temporal.io).

title: Decisions behind Go SDK not using Rust Core SDK
